question_text: What happens when Cl₂ reacts with a) slaked lime b) NaI?

verification.note: Unit 9 (VIIA Group Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.86-89, the sub-box "VIIA GROUP ELEMENTS" of printed chapter 7, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK TYPO (book p.86, VSAQ 5): the question is printed "Slakedlime" as one word; it is written "slaked lime" here. BOOK GAP: the printed answer does not say that the slaked lime must be DRY. With a solution of Ca(OH)₂ the products are calcium chloride and calcium hypochlorite, not bleaching powder, so the word dry is written on this card. Both printed equations were atom-counted and balance as printed.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: With slaked lime
lines: Chlorine passed over dry slaked lime gives
CaOCl₂ is bleaching powder. It is also
steps.why: The lime must be dry. With a solution of Ca(OH)₂ the chlorine disproportionates in the water and gives calcium chloride and calcium hypochlorite instead of bleaching powder, so the word dry is part of the answer. The equation balances with 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H and 2 Cl on each side.
common_mistakes: Writing CaCl₂ as the product. Bleaching powder is CaOCl₂ and keeps one oxygen atom.
Leaving out the water on the right. The two hydrogen atoms of Ca(OH)₂ have to appear somewhere.
steps.memory_tip: Dry lime plus chlorine gives bleaching powder; wet lime does not.
steps.margin_note: The balanced equation with CaOCl₂ named as bleaching powder is the whole of this mark.

steps.label: With sodium iodide
lines: Chlorine passed into a solution of sodium
Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than
iodine, so it displaces iodine from the salt.
steps.why: This is a displacement, and it works because of the oxidising order F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂, which runs steadily down the group with no exception. Chlorine takes the electron from I⁻, so Cl⁻ and free I₂ are formed. Any halogen displaces every halogen below it in the group from its salt.
common_mistakes: Writing NaCl₂ or NaI₂. Sodium is always +1, so the salts are NaCl and NaI.
Writing that iodine displaces chlorine. The halogen higher in the group displaces the one below it.
steps.memory_tip: Higher in the group displaces lower. Chlorine is above iodine, so iodine comes out.
steps.margin_note: The balanced equation earns the mark; the words "stronger oxidising agent" are what an examiner looks for beside it.

insider_note: Both parts are one balanced equation each. The word dry in part (a) and the words stronger oxidising agent in part (b) are what separate a full answer from a half one.
